newsitem.title: ITALY: Officials prepare world food summit documents.
newsitem.headline: Officials prepare world food summit documents.

text.p: Officials met on Monday to hammer out wording of two documents to be issued by the U.N. World Food Summit in Rome next month -- a labourious process of semantics, grammar and special interests.

The working group session hopes to reach agreement on all disputed language by Wednesday so that the "Rome Declaration on World Security" and the "Plan of Action" can be adopted without controversy at the summit from November 13 to 17.
The Rome-based U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) is sponsoring the conference at which an estimated 100 heads of state or government are expected for the final two days.
The meeting, whose slogan is "Food for All", aims to call attention to global hunger and find ways to distribute the world's resources more evenly.

The working group has to decide on 179 disputed phrases which have been bracketed in 31 pages of text. The officials began with less controversial elements, leaving contested language regarding trade and population issues for later.

For example, all parties agreed without dissent to remove an extraneous comma from the text and to change a phrase regarding the decline of official development assistance to "in recent years" from "in the last years."

The officials did not immediately address the disputed opening line of the declaration, which under a proposed version "reaffirms the right of every human being to have access to safe and nutritious food."
Some rich countries, such as the United States, fear that enshrining food as a "right" could lead to lawsuits demanding aid or special trade provisions.

The officials have yet to decide how to handle population issues and reproductive rights. FAO officials hoped to steer clear of this political hot potato, but special interest groups are pushing to place it high on the agenda.

"Women, who make up 50 percent of the world's population, are the front-line managers of food security in the home," said Dianne Dillon-Ridgley, a member of the U.S. delegation and president of the U.S. chapter of the group Zero Population Growth.
She said the food summit documents must, "at a minimum", contain language on reproductive rights agreed at previous U.N. summits such as last year's Beijing women's conference.
But Archbishop Alois Wagner, the Vatican's representative to FAO, said the summit should focus on reversing poverty and finding ways to make developing countries more self-sufficient.
The Vatican and developed countries including the United States and European nations clashed over the issue of reproductive rights at the 1994 U.N. population in Cairo.
